UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
 
)

LIMITED PROTEST OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or 
“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
(“Constellation”) hereby submits this limited protest of the revisions PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(“PJM”) submitted on July 31, 2026, to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and 
the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).2 
Constellation has serious concerns with several elements of the RBP, including its new-
resource limitations, pay-as-bid procurement structure, and cost-allocation consequences.  Given 
the need for prompt action, however, this limited protest seeks four targeted modifications and/or 
clarifications.  The first and most important is for the Commission to reject PJM’s proposal that 
“Available RBP UCAP” 3 participate in Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Auctions as a price 
taker for the duration of the RBP commitment.4  PJM suggests that RBP resources must be offered

2 
into RPM as a price-taker to ensure load does not “double pay” for capacity.  PJM’s proposal will 
do more harm than good, however, because it will undermine RPM’s ability to send accurate 
resource adequacy price signals in the future.5  As explained in Section I and the accompanying 
Affidavit of Roy J. Shanker, Ph.D., included here as Appendix A, PJM’s proposed requirement is 
not a just and reasonable means of addressing PJM’s asserted duplicate-procurement concern.  
Instead, Section I herein outlines why the Commission should direct PJM to exclude Available 
RBP UCAP from RPM price formation with a matched exclusion of RBP-Related Load.6  Such 
an annual isolation mechanism that adjusts both RBP supply and the matched quantity of RBP-
Related Load while preserving the RBP resources’ compensation and physical obligations is 
reflected in the Tariff language contained in Appendix B to this limited protest. 7  This modest 
adjustment to PJM’s proposal will allow the RBP to procure the megawatts needed to address 
PJM’s immediate resource adequacy shortfall, while preserving RPM’s effectiveness for price 
formation in support of long-term resource adequacy. 
Sections II through IV describe three additional changes that FERC must make to render 
the filing just and reasonable: (1) the deletion of the “new Maximum Facility Output” requirement 
in Tariff section 18.5(b)(i) and inclusion of qualifying Energy Resources in section 18.5(b)(iii); 
(2) the addition of a meaningful cure period for Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW submissions; 
and (3) clarification and revision of certain credit and collateral provisions. 
 
5  Id. at 57. 
6  “RBP-Related Load” means the portion of the incremental-load cohort used to establish or allocate the RBP that 
PJM includes in the planning parameters for the applicable RPM Auction. 
7  The proposed, illustrative language in Appendix B regarding the isolation mechanism is provided to assist the 
Commission in exercising its authority (to which PJM consented) to modify the proposed Tariff pursuant to the FPA 
and NRG Power Marketing in order to resolve the issues raised in this limited protest.  See, e.g., PJM Proposal at 3-4 
and 130-131.  No severance is recommended and effectuating Appendix B may be done and meshed with the other 
parts of the Tariff without causing delay in the commencement of the RBP in September 2026.

3 
Accordingly, consistent with NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC,8 the Commission 
should accept the RBP subject to the exercise of its authority to modify the proposed Tariff 
language in order to effectuate the four targeted Tariff and RAA modifications set forth herein and 
in Appendix B. 
I. 
LIMITED PROTEST OF REQUIREMENT THAT AVAILABLE RBP UCAP 
MUST OFFER INTO RPM AS A PRICE TAKER 
A. 
Introduction and Summary 
The capacity challenge facing the PJM Region is serious.9  While PJM’s filing includes 
several imperfections, Constellation does not oppose PJM’s use of a one-time RBP to address the 
shortfall in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction (“BRA”), reduced as applicable for accepted 
offsets and opt-outs.10 
Although PJM frames the RBP as a one-time stopgap measure, the zero-offer obligation 
will affect repeated RPM Auctions for as long as fifteen years.11  The RBP may address an 
immediate procurement need, but without modification it can weaken the market’s ability to attract 
and retain the capacity PJM will need in later years.  PJM’s price-taker requirement is unsupported 
and potentially harmful because it impairs RPM as a credible price-forming market.  Such 
degradation to RPM could result in resources deferring market entry or capital expenditures, 
exporting to other markets, or accelerating retirements—undermining the express resource 
adequacy purpose of PJM’s RBP proposal.12  
 
8  NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017).  
9  This limited protest does not challenge PJM’s decision to procure needed capacity or to impose enforceable physical 
performance obligations on selected resources. 
10  See PJM Proposal at 7–9. 
11  See id. at 5, 7.  
12 PJM itself has said RPM pricing below the value placed on capacity by other regions incents generators to export 
to neighboring regions.  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C, 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Reserve Target Shortfall

4 
As Dr. Roy Shanker—an economist with more than 50 years of electric-industry 
experience and approximately 30 years of competitive-market-design experience, including 
participation in PJM market design since RPM’s inception—explains: When Available RBP 
UCAP precedes or exceeds the RBP-Related Load reflected in an RPM Auction, the mandatory 
zero-offer rule can cause RPM to signal excess supply to the residual market.13  Distorting the 
RPM price signal threatens increased retirement risk, incents resources to export to other 
markets,14 and delays market entry and capital investment—leaving PJM short yet again when 
delayed load arrives.15  The risk of delayed load is real and looming, so ensuring RPM sends 
correct price signals, rather than promoting the exit of existing generation, is of critical importance 
to reliability. 
PJM has not addressed the foreseeable mismatch between supply and load timing.  PJM 
has supported the physical retention and compensation of RBP resources, but it has not shown 
that requiring those resources to offer at zero in RPM auctions will support resource adequacy in 
PJM beyond covering the most immediate shortfall.  That omission is the heart of this limited 
protest, and the solution lies in conditioning approval of PJM’s FPA 205 filing on the annual 
isolation mechanism that excludes the RBP resources and a matched quantity of RBP Load from 
RPM Auctions as set forth in Section I.D. 
 
Report 12 (Feb. 9, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-
2028/2027-2028-bra-reserve-target-shortfall-report.pdf.  
13  See Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 9, 14 
14 See, e.g., Cordova Energy Company LLC, 194 FERC 61,108 (2026) (authorizing a 611.2 MW natural-gas fueled, 
combined-cycle electric generating facility located in PJM to sell its capacity to an affiliate in MISO during the 
2028/2029 Delivery Year after already receiving approvals for similar sales during the 2027/2028 Delivery Year); 
Dairyland Power Coop., 194 FERC ¶ 61,133, at P 5 (2026) (explaining that Dairyland acquired PJM units for the 
purpose of exporting energy and capacity to fulfill Dairyland’s capacity obligations to its distribution cooperative 
members located in MISO). 
15  See Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 13–16.

5 
The PJM proposal aims to implement the Statement of Principles Regarding PJM issued 
on January 16, 2026, by the National Energy Dominance Council and the 13 governors of the PJM 
states.16  The NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles called both for prompt procurement and a return 
to market fundamentals.17  But mandatory zero offers for separately compensated RBP capacity 
frustrates that objective by causing RPM to signal excess supply when Available RBP UCAP 
exceeds RBP-Related Load that actually materializes.  The RBP proposed by PJM is not a return 
to market fundamentals but rather a retreat from them. 
It is wholly inconsistent with market fundamentals for the main capacity market, RPM, to 
falsely signal excess supply on the heels of a supplemental procurement due to a serious resource 
adequacy shortfall.  As Dr. Shanker explains, PJM’s proposed treatment of that capacity 
undermines the same resource-adequacy objective PJM aims to solve with the RBP.18 
B. 
PJM Has Not Shown That Mandatory Zero Offers Are Just and Reasonable 
PJM has shown why RBP resources should be retained for resource adequacy and why 
selected sellers should receive their accepted RBP compensation.  PJM has not shown why a zero 
price is the appropriate representation of those resources in the supply stack when RPM is intended 
to establish the marginal value of capacity.  
Whether an RBP resource should count toward reliability, whether it should receive its 
promised compensation, and whether its mandatory offer should affect the market price paid to 
non-RBP resources are distinct questions.  PJM’s filing conflates them in the name of guarding 
load against facing risk of double payment for capacity.  A mandatory $0/MW-day offer is not the 
 
16  PJM Proposal at 2 (citing National Energy Dominance Council, Statement of Principles Regarding PJM (Jan. 16, 
2026), 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm) 
(“NEDC/PJM 
Governors’ 
Principles”). 
17  NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles at 1. 
18  See Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 14–15.

6 
reasonable or just way to address that risk because such mandate does more harm than good by 
signaling excess supply if anticipated load is delayed or does not show up, thereby encouraging 
departure of existing generation—recreating the very reliability problems that spurred the RBP in 
the first place.  This problem can be eliminated, and load still protected from double payment, if 
instead PJM removes RBP supply while also removing the actual new load that the RBP resources 
were procured to supply.  That way, if anticipated load is delayed, the market will not signal excess 
supply and encourage retirement of the existing fleet. 
As Dr. Shanker explains, RPM price signals guide both new-entry and resource-retention 
decisions.19  When a large block of capacity procured under long-term, out-of-market 
commitments is required to offer at zero, prospective entrants may defer merchant investment in 
anticipation of lower-risk contractual opportunities, while existing resources may accelerate exit 
or decline to commit additional capital. 
Those responses can occur substantially faster than replacement generation can be 
developed.  An inappropriate signal today can therefore leave the competitive fleet smaller when 
forecast load ultimately arrives. 20  Indeed, Constellation suspects this phenomenon (lack of new 
entry and instead waiting for out-of-market compensation) was reflected in the last RPM auction, 
as the instant filing providing for an out-of-market auction opportunity was widely-discussed and 
expected. 
PJM’s own contemporaneous analysis corroborates Dr. Shanker.  PJM describes a 
“credibility trap” in which scarcity triggers price caps, emergency backstop procurements, or other 
 
19  Id. 
20  Id.

7 
administrative interventions.  Investors then discount the durability of the revenue signal, capital 
remains on the sidelines, and the shortage persists.21  
PJM states that the RBP should not subsume the broader review of market fundamentals 
and that the RBP should permit PJM to return to competitive resource-adequacy markets as soon 
as possible.22  Yet, the mandatory zero-offer requirement moves in the opposite direction by 
allowing the financial terms of a separate backstop procurement to determine the price signal 
received for the next 15 years by the residual competitive market, which could undermine the 
resource adequacy objective of that market. 
The challenged proposal is not transitory merely because PJM calls the RBP a “one-time” 
procurement.  The Initial RBP Target is 6,831.3 MW UCAP before accepted offsets and opt-outs. 
As selected resources become operational and accredited, PJM will require their committed, 
available RBP UCAP to offer at $0/MW-day in each applicable RPM Auction through the end of 
the applicable commitment (i.e., up to 15 years).  The procurement can create a potentially multi-
gigawatt block of mandatory zero-priced capacity in repeated RPM Auctions over many years. 
PJM supplies no sensitivity analysis evaluating whether its mandatory zero-offer rule will 
preserve appropriate entry and retention signals under plausible variations in timely load 
realization, resource commercial-operation dates, annual accreditation, resource exit or retirement, 
or updated Incremental Auction parameters.  Nor does PJM analyze the later resource-adequacy 
effect if delayed load arrives after the auction signal has induced exit or deferred entry.  PJM’s

22  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Critical Issue Fast Path–Reliability Backstop Procurement PJM Proposal 1(June 30,

section 205 showing therefore does not address the central price-formation and resource-adequacy 
consequences of the rule it proposes. 
C. 
The Risk Is Most Acute When Available RBP UCAP Precedes or Exceeds 
Timely RBP-Related Load 
The price-formation and reliability risks are most acute when Available RBP UCAP 
exceeds the RBP-Related Load included in the Planning Parameters for the applicable RPM 
Auction.  That mismatch does not require long-term load growth to disappear—a delay alone is 
sufficient.  Even if all forecast load ultimately connects, a multi-year delay can cause RPM to 
signal reduced need for resource retention and new entry before the load arrives. 
Dr. Shanker uses a simplified example in which the full Initial RBP Target is available in 
the relevant auction but load is delayed.23  This delayed-load example shows the resulting 
problem.24  Assume, for illustration, that approximately 6.8 GW of RBP capacity becomes 
available and must enter RPM at a zero price, but only 3 GW of RBP-Related Load is reflected in 
the applicable auction parameters due to large load delays.  RPM would then reflect 3.8 GW of 
unmatched zero-offer RBP supply without the corresponding RBP-Related Load.  That clearing 
outcome can signal reduced need for retention or entry in the RPM market.  If the remaining load 
arrives several years later, some existing capacity may already have retired (or otherwise exited 
PJM), and prospective new entry may have stayed on the sidelines.  Because retirement/exit can 
occur faster than replacement capacity can be developed, PJM may again face a shortfall and 
pressure for another out-of-market procurement.25 
 
23  In operation, the quantity of Available RBP UCAP subject to the isolation mechanism would vary by Delivery 
Year based on commercial-operation timing, accreditation, and availability, as described above. 
24  Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 13–14. 
25  Id. ¶¶ 14–16.

9 
PJM’s implementation design confirms that the relevant supply and demand quantities will 
vary across auctions.  Available RBP UCAP may ramp across several Delivery Years, while PJM 
will continue to update its load forecasts through later RPM Auctions.  PJM’s August 10 example, 
for instance, shows an illustrative 6,800 MW portfolio providing 3,900 MW in 2028/2029, 6,750 
MW in 2029/2030, 6,800 MW in 2030/2031, and 6,850 MW in 2031/2032.  PJM’s example is 
illustrative rather than predictive, but it confirms that the filed selection architecture permits RBP 
quantities to vary materially across Delivery Years and that RBP supply may exceed the target in 
a particular year.26  
Incremental Auctions do not cure this problem.  They update the competitive market 
around the RBP commitments; they do not true up or unwind the underlying backstop 
procurement.  If PJM lowers the load reflected in the planning parameters (even temporarily) while 
Available RBP UCAP remains subject to the zero-offer requirement, the forecast correction is 
borne by the existing resources participating in the RPM market rather than by the out-of-market 
procurement based on the earlier forecast.27 
The supply-load timing risk is not merely conceptual.  ERCOT has reported approximately 
8,900 MW of large load approved for energization, of which more than 5,000 MW had not yet 
energized, while significant new generation and storage capacity was being added.28  While 
ERCOT’s market design differs materially from PJM’s, this example illustrates an underlying 
factual risk:  large-load projects and new supply do not necessarily become operational on the 
 
26  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C and Charles River Associates, Reliability Backstop Procurement Execution 
Presentation, 44–45 (Aug. 10, 2026).  Slides 44-45 show 3,900 MW in 2028/2029, 6,750 MW in 2029/2030, 6,800 
MW in 2030/2031, and 6,850 MW in 2031/2032, and explain that full, indivisible offers may exceed the remaining 
target). 
27  Shanker Aff. ¶ 17. 
28  Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Large Load Interconnection Status Update, Large Load Integration Team 8–
9 (June 19, 2026), https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/06/18/June-19-LLWG-Report.pptx.

10 
same schedule.  Based on the ERCOT example, it is not a hypothetical that new supply may enter 
service prior to when the corresponding large load enters service.  PJM’s RBP design should not 
assume otherwise. 
PJM’s own recent downward revisions to its near-term load growth forecasts confirms that 
large-load forecasts are not static and that the amount reflected in successive RPM Auctions can 
change materially.  The downward revision for peak annual load in 2027 was trimmed by 3,735 
MW.29  The point is not that PJM’s long-term load growth will necessarily fail to appear.  The 
point is that the timing of supply and load can diverge long enough for a temporary RBP supply 
surplus to produce durable entry, exit, and retirement consequences in RPM.30 
When timely RBP-Related Load is below Available RBP UCAP, mandatory zero-offer 
RBP supply can cause RPM to signal excess supply to the RPM market before the forecast load 
has arrived, even as PJM expects delayed load to require additional capacity.  That signal bears 
directly on entry, retention, and capital-investment decisions and can leave PJM short precisely 
when PJM continues to forecast substantial future demand.  
D. 
Annual RBP Isolation and a Matched Demand Adjustment Will Preserve the 
Competitive Integrity of RPM While Avoiding Duplicate Procurement 
To prevent the adverse impacts described above, while still protecting customers from 
double payment for capacity, Dr. Shanker recommends isolation through an annual, auction-
specific mechanism.  Dr. Shanker recommends removing the separately procured RBP supply and 
 
29  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., PJM’s Updated 20-Year Forecast Continues to See Significant Long-Term Load 
Growth (Jan. 14, 2026), https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjms-updated-20-year-forecast-continues-to-see-significant-
long-term-load-growth/.  
30  Goldman Sachs reports that historically approximately 72% of data centers scheduled for activation within the 
following four quarters came online on time and forecasts on-time realization of approximately 60% over the next 
year and approximately 50% over the next two years.  See Goldman Sachs, US Data Center Power Demand Projected 
to Double by 2027 (May 20, 2026), https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/us-data-center-power-demand-
projected-to-double-by-2027.

11 
the corresponding RBP-related demand from RPM price formation.31  This isolation mechanism 
eliminates the threat of any double payment and removes the deleterious impact on RPM.  The 
Tariff language in Appendix B implements Dr. Shanker’s core isolation recommendation through 
an annual, auction-specific mechanism. 
The revisions in Appendix B translate that economic recommendation into the filed RBP 
design by accounting for annual accreditation, availability, commercial-operation timing, and the 
conduct of both Base Residual Auctions and Incremental Auctions.  For each Delivery Year and 
each applicable RPM Auction, PJM should: (1) exclude Available RBP UCAP from the RPM 
price-forming supply stack; and (2) reduce the applicable RPM reliability requirement by the lesser 
of Available RBP UCAP and RBP-Related Load included in the Planning Parameters for that 
auction, with both quantities expressed in UCAP terms.32 
The adjustment concerns price formation only.  The revisions in Appendix B preserve the 
RBP resources’ physical and performance obligations and the two-sided economics of the RBP 
settlement. 
PJM argues that zero-price participation is necessary because responsible LSEs already are 
paying for RBP capacity and another resource might otherwise be procured via RPM if the RBP 
resources are not entered as price-takers, resulting in a double payment for capacity by load.33  
That concern assumes RBP supply is removed while the entire associated demand requirement 
remains in RPM.  Constellation’s proposal does not do that.  For the matched quantity—the lesser 
of Available RBP UCAP and RBP-Related Load—the mechanism adjusts both supply and 
 
31  Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 25–30. 
32  Id. ¶ 25. 
33  PJM Proposal at 57.

12 
demand.  RPM therefore does not procure replacement capacity for load already covered through 
the RBP.34 
Dr. Shanker also explains why all RBP resources must be excluded, as price-taker offers 
cannot readily be prorated among individual large-load projects.  RBP resources are not physically 
matched to particular loads, and individual generating units cannot be divided among varying 
levels of realized load without creating another administrative allocation mechanism.35  The more 
workable design is to isolate all the RBP supply while adjusting demand by the amount of timely 
RBP-Related Load. 
Where Available RBP UCAP exceeds timely RBP-Related Load, Constellation recognizes 
that isolation may temporarily preserve more total physical capacity than the updated RPM 
requirement alone would procure.  Constellation proposes that result as a safeguard against 
allowing a potentially temporary, forecast-created mismatch to trigger exit and deferred 
investment before the load arrives.  The relevant comparison is intertemporal: temporary additional 
capacity versus premature exit, later replacement, another capacity shortfall, and another backstop 
procurement. 
PJM itself evaluated carving RBP supply and demand out of RPM.36  It anticipated that the 
capacity-cost outcomes of the zero-offer and carve-out approaches would be largely the same and 
that neither would materially change costs to the remaining RPM load.  PJM rejected isolation 
 
34  Even excluding the RBP supply and associated load as proposed here does not completely neutralize the out-of-
market effects on RPM, as RPM is deprived of the RBP resources that would sit at the top of the supply stack, 
providing upward pressure on RPM price signals.  See ISO New England Inc., 138 FERC ¶ 61,027 at PP 72–75 (2012); 
see also ISO New England Inc., 135 FERC ¶ 61,029 at PP 230, 232 (2011).  By this measure, the isolation methodology 
is a conservative solution, yet is significantly more effective at reducing any out-of-market pricing impact as compared 
to the mandatory zero offer proposal, and without creating any risk of double payment.  
35  Shanker Aff. ¶ 29. 
36  PJM Paper at 11.

13 
principally because it believed the approach would differentiate large load from other load and 
require additional changes to RPM.37 
That concession substantially narrows the dispute.  The RBP already creates a separately 
compensated supply cohort associated with a separately identified increment of forecast load for 
terms lasting as long as fifteen years.  Isolating that cohort from RPM price formation better 
preserves the competitive integrity of the residual market than requiring it to participate at zero in 
every applicable RPM Auction. 
RBP isolation and the matched demand adjustment therefore preserve the RBP 
procurement and the physical availability of RBP resources without representing separately 
compensated capacity as though its competitive RPM offer were zero. 
II. 
THE PHRASE “MAXIMUM FACILITY OUTPUT” IN TARIFF SECTION 
18.5(b)(i) SHOULD BE DELETED, AND ENERGY RESOURCES SHOULD BE 
INCLUDED IN SECTION 18.5(b)(iii). 
The Commission should condition acceptance of PJM’s Proposal on (A) revising proposed 
Tariff section 18.5(b)(i) from “new Installed Capacity and new Maximum Facility Output” to “new 
Installed Capacity” and (B) revising proposed Tariff section 18.5(b)(iii)(2) to include an Energy 
Resource seeking new Capacity Interconnection Rights.  As drafted, section 18.5(b) excludes an 
existing Energy Resource that has Maximum Facility Output but no Capacity Interconnection 
Rights and is seeking new Capacity Interconnection Rights through an Interconnection Request, 
even if the resource otherwise satisfies the RBP eligibility criteria. 
To qualify as an RBP Resource, a generation resource must meet the requirements of 
sections 18.5(a) and 18.5(b) of the proposed Tariff.  Such generation resources must have a

14 
commercial operation date prior to June 1, 2032, not otherwise have an RPM commitment for a 
future delivery year, and be: 
(i) Composed of new Installed Capacity and new Maximum Facility Output; 
(ii) Supported by new Capacity Interconnection Rights (if located in the 
PJM Region) or Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred from a 
deactivated resource or a resource that announced deactivation as of April 
10, 2026; and 
(iii) Consist of (1) new build; (2) incremental capacity created by an uprate 
of an existing Generation Capacity Resource’s or Energy Storage 
Resource’s installed capacity and associated level of Capacity 
Interconnection Rights; or (3) repowering of a generation resource that had 
deactivated, or announced deactivation, on or before April 10, 2026.38 
An existing Energy Resource necessarily has Maximum Facility Output; obtaining new 
Capacity Interconnection Rights does not create a new Maximum Facility Output.  The relevant 
attribute from a resource adequacy perspective is the new Capacity Interconnection Rights.  
Excluding an otherwise eligible resource solely because its Maximum Facility Output is not “new” 
and because it is currently not a capacity resource but is seeking to obtain new Capacity 
Interconnection Rights is unjust and unreasonable where the resource will provide new capacity, 
satisfy the applicable commercial-operation requirements, and bear its share of any required 
Network Upgrade costs associated with securing its new Capacity Interconnection Rights. 
Accordingly, the Commission should exercise its authority to modify the proposed Tariff 
language to delete the phrase “and new Maximum Facility Output” in proposed Tariff section 
18.5(b)(i) and add Energy Resources seeking new Capacity Interconnection Rights as a category 
of resource eligible under section 18.5(b)(iii)(2).

III. 
QUALIFYING RBP OFFSET UCAP MW SUBMISSIONS SHOULD RECEIVE A 
MEANINGFUL CURE PERIOD 
Constellation requests clarification that PJM will provide a submitting entity five calendar 
days from notice to cure a deficiency in a Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW submission, provided 
that the cure is completed before the close of the bid submission window of the Reliability 
Backstop Procurement.  If PJM does not confirm that interpretation, the Commission should 
condition acceptance on Tariff revisions expressly providing that cure opportunity. 
New Section 18.2(c) requires entities to report the Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW 
during the RBP bid submission window with accompanying listed evidence, but does not explicitly 
provide for a cure period upon a finding of deficiency by PJM.39  PJM has indicated in stakeholder 
workshops that it would initiate discussions with any parties where there are questions regarding 
the submission of evidence of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.  Further, PJM’s recently-
proposed draft Manual 18 Attachment F confirms that PJM contemplates that there will be some 
level of communication with participants regarding clarification of evidence submitted by 
participants seeking to establish Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.40  However, given the impact 
of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW on the RBP’s total procurement target and the procurement 
assignment and allocation of charges to specific EDC zones/areas, a more formal and explicit cure 
process is warranted. 
RBP Sell Offers receive a five-calendar-day cure opportunity after notice of a deficiency.41  
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW submissions should receive the same substantive protection. 
The Commission should therefore exercise its authority to modify the proposed Tariff language to

before the close of the bid submission window of the Reliability Backstop Procurement.  This

IV. 
LIMITED PROTEST OF CERTAIN CREDIT AND COLLATERAL PROVISIONS 
The Commission should exercise its authority to modify the proposed Tariff language to 
clarify two aspects of the credit and collateral provisions in the proposed Tariff. 
First, the Commission should clarify that, for purposes of proposed Tariff section 18.8, 
reference to “the first Delivery Year” means the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.  As written, the phrase 
is ambiguous and does not provide affected Load Serving Entities sufficient certainty regarding 
the date on which the initial collateral obligation attaches. 
Second, in section 18.3(b)(iii) of the proposed Tariff, the Commission should replace the 
phrase “no later than sixty (60) days prior to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year” with “no later than 
three-hundred sixty-five (365) days prior to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.”  This would allow 
market participants to have a clear understanding of how the initial allocation determination under 
section 18.3 will be effectuated, and perhaps equally important, how any default amounts that 
result from the failure of expected large loads to materialize will also be allocated.  This timeline

Recommendation 
24. 
The preferred approach for any market design would be to adopt a design that works 
without the need for ad-hoc interventions and stick with that design—both when prices rise and 
when they fall.  The dislocation caused by the combination of large new loads, regulatory and 
political intervention, and the continued erosion of true market-based pricing makes that solution 
very unlikely. But if PJM must intervene now with an ad-hoc intervention such as the RBP out-
of-market procurement, a top priority of the intervention should be to preserve resource adequacy 
by maintaining the competitive integrity of the overall market going forward to the greatest extent 
possible.  Without that focus it is very likely that PJM will see increased exits of existing resources 
(which will only exacerbate resource adequacy issues in the region) and be right back at the

25. 
To that end, my recommendation is to modify the RBP proposal to include a 
mechanism that will appropriately isolate the effect of the RBP and maintain appropriate 
investment signals for the remainder of the capacity market.  There is a very simple way to 
accomplish this objective. Rather than requiring all RBP supply to offer into RPM at $0/MW-day, 
PJM should remove all RBP supply and RBP-related demand from the RPM Auctions going 
forward.  Specifically, PJM should exclude from RPM Auctions both (a) the cleared RBP capacity 
and (b) the lower of (i) the actual large load that is in the applicable auction Planning Parameters 
and (ii) an amount of load equal to the RBP generation. 
26. 
This representation is as neutral as possible with respect to price formation for the 
“rest” of the market, and allows PJM to return to market fundamentals, market-based procurement, 
and rates and avoid unnecessary exits of existing resources. With this adjustment in place the rest 
of the market sees the “right” representation of supply and demand. And in this manner the market 
can adjust going forward independently of PJM’s “one-time” RBP purchases. In turn, regardless 
of the rate of arrival of the 6,800 MW of demand (the forecasted deficiency), there will be no price 
distortion for the rest of the market. The RBP capacity will operate as intended, as a separate out-
of-market procurement to assure reliability.  
27. 
When seen in light of PJM’s removal of future large loads, my recommendation to 
simply remove both the RBP supply and the lower of (i) the actual large load that is in the 
applicable auction Planning Parameters and (ii) an amount of load equal to the RBP generation 
becomes almost obvious in terms of logical consistency. Failing to make the adjustment discussed 
herein leaves the PJM proposal fundamentally discriminatory against existing suppliers who

arrive completely. 
28. 
In this context it is illogical to not remove all out-of-market RBP supply and 
the associated demand. Doing so removes the asymmetry and any associated price distortion. 
With this proposal the RBP procurement exists and continues to address reliability. But my 
recommended adjustment prevents delays in the arrival of the forecast demand or the failure of the 
forecast demand (the 6,800 MW) to enter at all from artificially shifting prices. The rest of the 
market therefore sees accurate price signals. 
29. 
It is important to understand that this must be achieved by isolating this RBP load 
and generation. This is because the RBP generation is not readily divisible, e.g. it cannot be 
reasonably pro-rated for participation vis-a-vis any specific load. It must be either in or out. There 
is not a simple way to pro-rate a half of such a unit’s participation in the context of varying levels 
of realized load. Thus, the correct approach is to simply remove both the out-of-market supply and 
the realized portion of the load it was intended to serve. Modifying the demand curve by the same 
(reliability adjusted) amount in either direction does not distort prices. There is no reason to retain 
the one-way bias that PJM has built into the representation of the RBP supply when the bias and 
price distortion can be so easily fixed.

a procurement, this type of isolation is necessary to protect the markets and stands independently 
as a required feature.

18.10 Annual RBP Isolation and Matched Demand Adjustment 
(a) Applicability 
For each Delivery Year during the Reliability Backstop Procurement commitment period, and 
for each Base Residual Auction and Incremental Auction conducted after the Office of the 
Interconnection commits RBP UCAP MW through the Reliability Backstop Procurement, the 
Office of the Interconnection shall apply the RBP isolation and matched demand adjustment set 
forth in this section. 
(b) Determination of Available RBP UCAP MW 
Before posting the Planning Parameters for each applicable RPM Auction, the Office of the 
Interconnection shall determine Available RBP UCAP MW for the applicable Delivery Year on 
a resource-specific and aggregate basis. The determination shall account for the RBP Resource’s 
committed RBP UCAP MW, applicable Accredited UCAP, expected commercial-operation or 
registration status, deliverability, any notice submitted pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, 
section 5.5, approved replacement capacity, and any rescission pursuant to Tariff, Attachment 
DD, section 18.6(e). 
The Office of the Interconnection shall determine Available RBP UCAP MW for the PJM 
Region and by Zone and modeled Locational Deliverability Area. 
(c) Determination of RBP-Related Load UCAP MW 
Before posting the Planning Parameters for each applicable RPM Auction, the Office of the 
Interconnection shall determine the portion of the incremental-load cohort used to establish or 
allocate the Reliability Backstop Procurement that is included in the Planning Parameters for the 
applicable RPM Auction. The Office of the Interconnection shall convert such load to UCAP 
MW using the Forecast Pool Requirement and the existing methodologies used to determine the 
applicable PJM Region and LDA Reliability Requirements. 
The determination shall exclude load associated with Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, 
approved opt-outs, FRR Entities, and load not included in the applicable RPM Auction Planning 
Parameters. Load shall not be counted more than once under this section or under any other 
Tariff provision providing for exclusion or matched treatment of New Large Load. 
(d) RTO-Wide RBP Demand Adjustment 
For each applicable RPM Auction, the RBP Demand Adjustment for the PJM Region shall equal 
the lesser of: 
1. Available RBP UCAP MW; and  
2. RBP-Related Load UCAP MW included in the Planning Parameters for such RPM 
Auction.

2 
 
Solely for purposes of clearing and price formation in the applicable RPM Auction, the Office of 
the Interconnection shall reduce the PJM Region Reliability Requirement by the RBP Demand 
Adjustment. 
(e) Exclusion of Available RBP UCAP MW 
Available RBP UCAP MW shall not be included in any Sell Offer, price-forming supply curve, 
or optimization used to determine the Capacity Resource Clearing Price in an applicable RPM 
Auction. Available RBP UCAP MW shall not clear such RPM Auction and shall not receive 
RPM Auction capacity credits. 
Any UCAP MW of an RBP Resource above its committed RBP UCAP MW may participate in 
RPM Auctions pursuant to otherwise applicable Tariff and RAA requirements. 
To the extent Available RBP UCAP MW exceeds RBP-Related Load UCAP MW, such excess 
shall remain excluded from RPM Auction price formation and shall not produce an additional 
reduction in any RPM reliability requirement. 
(f) Incremental Auctions 
For each Incremental Auction, the Office of the Interconnection shall recalculate Available RBP 
UCAP MW, RBP-Related Load UCAP MW, and the RBP Demand Adjustment using the 
updated Planning Parameters for the applicable Delivery Year. The RBP-Adjusted Reliability 
Requirement used in the Incremental Auction shall reflect the recalculated RBP Demand 
Adjustment and all RPM commitments established in prior RPM Auctions for the same Delivery 
Year. Available RBP UCAP MW shall not be included as an RPM commitment established in a 
prior auction. 
(g) Locational Treatment 
The Office of the Interconnection shall allocate the RBP Demand Adjustment among Zones 
based on the location of RBP-Related Load included in the applicable Planning Parameters. 
For each modeled LDA, the reduction in the LDA Reliability Requirement shall not exceed: 
1. RBP-Related Load UCAP MW located in such LDA; or  
2. Available RBP UCAP MW located in, or determined under the same CETO and CETL 
assumptions used in the applicable RPM Auction to be deliverable to, such LDA.  
The Office of the Interconnection shall not count the same RBP Demand Adjustment more than 
once among nested LDAs and their parent LDAs. Any portion of the RTO-wide RBP Demand 
Adjustment that cannot support an LDA adjustment under this subsection shall not reduce the 
reliability requirement for that LDA.

3 
(h) Publication
With the Planning Parameters for each applicable RPM Auction, the Office of the 
Interconnection shall post the aggregate Available RBP UCAP MW, RBP-Related Load UCAP 
MW, RBP Demand Adjustment, and resulting RBP-Adjusted Reliability Requirements for the 
PJM Region and each affected Zone and LDA. Resource- or customer-specific confidential 
information may be omitted from the public posting but shall be made available to the Market 
Monitoring Unit. 
(i) Effect Limited to RPM Price Formation
The exclusion of Available RBP UCAP MW under this section shall not relieve an RBP 
Resource of any accreditation, deliverability, registration, testing, outage-reporting, energy-
market must-offer, Capacity Performance, replacement-capacity, Non-Performance Charge, 
deficiency-charge, RBP shortfall, or other physical or performance obligation applicable to the 
committed RBP UCAP MW. 
Recommended new and revised defined terms 
“Available RBP UCAP MW” shall mean, for an RPM Auction for a Delivery Year, the 
aggregate UCAP MW of RBP Resources committed for such Delivery Year that the Office of the 
Interconnection determines, using the accreditation, commercial-operation or registration, 
deliverability, and availability standards that otherwise would apply in determining the quantity 
of such resources eligible to participate in that RPM Auction, are expected to be available to 
provide capacity during such Delivery Year; provided that Available RBP UCAP MW shall not 
exceed the RBP UCAP MW committed for such Delivery Year and shall exclude any 
commitment rescinded pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.6(e). 
“RBP-Related Load UCAP MW” shall mean, for an RPM Auction for a Delivery Year, 
exclusive of any load associated with Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, an approved opt-out, 
an FRR Entity, or load otherwise excluded from the applicable RPM Auction Planning 
Parameters, the sum of all Large Loads across the PJM region in the load forecast for the 
relevant Delivery Year minus the sum of all Large Loads across the PJM region that were 
forecasted to be on the system for the 2026/27 delivery year using the load forecast that was used 
for the 2028/29 Base Residual Auction. Peak-load megawatts shall be converted to UCAP MW 
using the Forecast Pool Requirement and the applicable existing zonal and LDA methodologies 
for such Delivery Year. 
“RBP Demand Adjustment” shall mean, for an RPM Auction for a Delivery Year, the lesser of 
Available RBP UCAP MW and RBP-Related Load UCAP MW, as determined and allocated to 
the PJM Region, Zones, and affected Locational Deliverability Areas in accordance with Tariff, 
Attachment DD, section 18.10.

4 
 
“RBP-Adjusted Reliability Requirement” shall mean, solely for purposes of clearing and price 
formation in an RPM Auction, the applicable PJM Region Reliability Requirement or LDA 
Reliability Requirement, as applicable, reduced by the RBP Demand Adjustment determined 
pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.10. The RBP-Adjusted Reliability Requirement 
shall not modify the applicable reliability criterion, Forecast Pool Requirement, or physical 
resource-adequacy requirement. 
“Daily RBP Settlement Quantity” shall mean, for an RBP Resource and Operating Day, the 
lesser of the RBP Resource’s daily committed RBP UCAP MW and daily owned UCAP MW. 
“RBP Market Revenue Offset” shall mean, for a Delivery Year and Electric Distributor 
zone/area, the daily dollar value of the final RBP Demand Adjustment allocated to such 
zone/area multiplied by the applicable Final Zonal Capacity Price, subject to interim calculation 
and true-up as set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(g). 
“RBP Settlement Credits” shall mean the daily dollar amount payable to an RBP Resource 
pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(g), before application of any RBP shortfall 
charge, Non-Performance Charge, deficiency charge, or other applicable charge. 
“RBP Charges” shall mean the daily positive or negative net amount determined pursuant to 
Tariff, Attachment DD, sections 18.3 and 18.5(g), consisting of RBP Settlement Credits allocated 
to an Electric Distributor zone/area, less the RBP Market Revenue Offset applicable to such 
zone/area, together with any other adjustment expressly included pursuant to Tariff, Attachment 
DD, section 18.
